llm_response.content:
COMPLETE EMPIRICAL PLAN  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy chosen: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with heterogeneous treatment intensity.

Why DID fits here  
• We have two dimensions of variation: (i) time – whether a trading day is a scheduled macro-announcement day, and (ii) cross-section – the level of ex-ante market beta for each stock (or beta-sorted portfolio).  
• The causal quantity of interest is the incremental return that higher-beta stocks earn specifically on announcement days relative to otherwise similar non-announcement days.  
• A DID that interacts the announcement-day dummy with the continuous beta measure (or with high- vs. low-beta group dummies) delivers exactly that estimand while controlling for time-invariant firm characteristics and day-specific common shocks via fixed effects.  
• Repeated, known-in-advance announcements give us hundreds of quasi-experiments, making the panel DID (α_i + γ_t) attractive and powerful.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
A daily indicator ANN_t that equals 1 if day t is one of the three scheduled macro release days (Employment, CPI, or FOMC) and 0 otherwise.

Treatment intensity  
The continuous, pre-estimated one-year rolling CAPM beta β_i (or discrete beta-quintile dummies). In the DID we use ANN_t × β_i.

Control group / counterfactual  
• Same stocks on non-announcement days (within-stock comparison) supply the main counterfactual.  
• Low-beta stocks on announcement days supply a secondary cross-sectional counterfactual.

Treatment timing  
Treatment occurs on the calendar dates released ex ante by BLS and the Fed; the market cannot choose them, ruling out timing endogeneity.

No running variable – not an RDD design.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends (or parallel conditional means)  
Absent macro announcements, the expected return difference between high- and low-beta stocks would have been the same on announcement and non-announcement days. Because the announcements are scheduled and unrelated to contemporaneous firm-level shocks, this is plausible, but we will test for it with placebo days and pre-event leads.

A2. No anticipatory or delayed effects outside the event window  
If information leaks before the 9:30/8:30 release or drifts afterward, the risk premium might spill into adjacent days and bias estimates. We will use 1-day and ±15-minute intraday windows as robustness checks.

A3. Exogeneity of β_i classification  
Betas are estimated using only past data, so they are predetermined with respect to future announcements. Measurement error in beta biases coefficients toward zero but does not create spurious positives.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers)  
An announcement affects the whole market at once; it does not differentially alter the counterfactual returns of low-beta stocks other than through market-wide price moves already controlled for by γ_t.

A5. Correct functional form / linearity  
The DID assumes the β_i interaction captures the relevant heterogeneity. We will verify robustness to non-parametric beta-spline and quintile-dummy specifications.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations  

Threat 1: Concurrent unscheduled firm-specific or sectoral news might cluster on the same calendar days (e.g., first Friday of the month for employment coinciding with earnings seasons).  
Mitigation:  
• Include firm-level earnings-announcement dummies and sector×day fixed effects.  
• Re-estimate dropping the ±3 days around quarterly earnings.  

Threat 2: Liquidity and volatility spikes on announcement days could mechanically raise measured returns via bid-ask bounce or increased risk, not compensated risk.  
Mitigation:  
• Use close-to-close, open-to-close, and mid-quote returns.  
• Control for daily VIX and volume; re-run on larger, more liquid subsample (top size decile).  

Threat 3: Beta measurement error / regression dilution.  
Mitigation:  
• Shrink betas with the Vasicek/Bayes adjustment.  
• Aggregate into beta-sorted portfolios (value-weighted); run portfolio-level DID which eliminates individual beta noise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast io
library(fixest)       # high-dim fixed effects
library(lubridate)    # dates
library(sandwich)     # vcov
library(modelsummary) # reporting

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------
ret   <- fread("crsp_daily_returns.csv")        # permno, date, ret
beta  <- fread("daily_betas.csv")               # permno, date, beta
ann   <- fread("macro_announcement_dates.csv")  # date, emp, cpi, fomc
ff3   <- fread("fama_french_factors.csv")       # date, mktrf, smb, hml, rf

# 2. Merge and construct vars ---------------------------------------
ann[, ANN := as.integer(emp == 1 | cpi == 1 | fomc == 1)]
data <- merge(ret, beta, by = c("permno","date"))
data <- merge(data, ann[, .(date, ANN)], by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
data <- merge(data, ff3[, .(date, rf)], by = "date", all.x = TRUE)

data[is.na(ANN), ANN := 0]
data[, excess_ret := ret - rf]     # CAPM excess return

# 3. Main DID regression --------------------------------------------
# r_it = alpha_i + gamma_t + theta*beta_i + lambda*ANN_t + delta*ANN_t*beta_i + eps

did <- feols(excess_ret ~ beta + ANN + ANN:beta |
               permno + date, data = data,
             cluster = ~permno + date)   # 2-way clustering

etable(did, se = "cluster")

# 4. Robustness: portfolio-level, value-weighted quintiles ----------

# build quintiles each June t-1
data[, beta_q := cut(beta,
                     quantile(beta, probs = 0:5/5, na.rm = TRUE),
                     labels = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE),
     by = .(year = year(date), month = month(date) >= 7)]
# value-weighted return
port <- data[, .(vwret = weighted.mean(excess_ret, w = mktcap, na.rm = TRUE)),
             by = .(date, beta_q, ANN)]
fe <- feols(vwret ~ ANN | beta_q + date,
            data = port, cluster = ~beta_q + date)
etable(fe, se = "cluster")

# 5. Placebo: “pseudo-announcement” days one week earlier -----------
ann[, PLAC := as.integer(ANN == 1)]
ann[, date := date - 7]  # shift 7 days earlier
data <- merge(data, ann[, .(date, PLAC)], by = "date", all.x = TRUE)
data[is.na(PLAC), PLAC := 0]

placebo <- feols(excess_ret ~ PLAC:beta | permno + date,
                 data = data, cluster = ~permno + date)
etable(placebo, se = "cluster")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Economic prior: δ = Cov(β, return)|ANN − Cov(β, return)|nonANN > 0.  
Magnitude: Suppose the unconditional beta-return slope is roughly zero post-1963 (Fama-French). If the full annual risk premium of ~6% is realized on ±35 announcement days per year, the daily premium on those days should be ≈ 6%/35 ≈ 17 bp per unit beta. Given β dispersion (~0.3 between quintiles), we expect high-minus-low quintile excess return ≈ 5-6 bp per announcement day, translating to ~1.5% annualized, while the same difference on non-announcement days should be statistically indistinguishable from zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  

C1: Exogeneity of treatment timing (scheduled releases) …… 1  
C2: Parallel trends between groups absent treatment ……… 0.8  
C3: No interference / spillovers ……………………………………… 0.9  
C4: No differential composition changes over time ………… 0.8  
C5: Correct model & time-varying confounders controlled … 0.8  

Total (out of 5) = 4.3 → “good but not bulletproof.”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan delivers a clean, intuitive test of whether the market compensates systematic risk precisely when macroeconomic information is resolved, using a transparent DID framework and multiple robustness checks.
